governanceNotes: Authored conservatively at ASSOCIATION_ONLY strength: the defining clinical literature itself names bladder/bowel dysfunction among the presenting signs of conus medullaris syndrome, but the quantified evidence base is case-series class (Chiu & Liao 2019: 8 patients) without population denominators or onset-ordering, so no causal claim is forced at the mapping level; the signature is the pattern of the syndrome, not an independent claim the veteran must separately prove by population statistics.

Etiologic heterogeneity is preserved: conus medullaris syndrome arises from traumatic burst fractures, disc herniation, spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas, tumors, and ischemia (Stevens 2009 case documents an occult DAVF presenting as rapidly progressive conus syndrome with urinary retention and fecal incontinence); the downstream incontinence edges inherit that heterogeneity, which is why aggravation was not drafted.

Sibling-consistency note: this edge is tiered identically to the anterior-cord-syndrome -> urinary-incontinence association-only precedent (ME-32) and the central-cord-syndrome -> urinary-incontinence batch-9 draft, keeping the incomplete-spinal-cord-syndrome family internally consistent.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The defining-presentation and case-series literature documents bladder dysfunction as a core feature of conus medullaris syndrome: the pure-conus surgical cohort (8 patients, L1 burst fractures) recorded urodynamic-confirmed neurogenic bladder in all patients, split between overactive and underactive types, with only half regaining normal voiding function at final follow-up (Chiu & Liao 2019); the lumbar burst-fracture case study documents bladder dysfunction from conus injury after a 25-foot fall (Storch 2005); the DAVF case report presents urinary retention as part of a rapidly progressive conus syndrome (Stevens 2009).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the quantified evidence is a single 8-patient surgical series plus case reports, the injury-level-to-bladder-phenotype mapping varies patient to patient, and the neurogenic-bladder literature defines the dysfunction as a direct expression of the lesion rather than an independently progressing condition, so only co-occurrence within the syndrome picture is recorded.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A sacral-segment-injury pathway is hypothesized: the conus medullaris houses the S2-S4 sacral micturition center, so a lesion compressing or destroying the conus (burst fracture retropulsion, venous congestive myelopathy, mass effect) interrupts supraspinal and parasympathetic bladder control simultaneously, producing urodynamic patterns ranging from detrusor overactivity with urge incontinence to detrusor areflexia with retention and overflow incontinence depending on whether the injury is irritative or destructive at the segment; recovery depends on residual viable tissue rather than a progressive process. The mechanism is anatomically direct and treatment-validated (the neurogenic-bladder management literature exists precisely because of this lesion class), but the mapping-level evidence is case-series class without denominators, so only association is claimed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Bladder dysfunction co-occurs as a defining feature of conus medullaris syndrome across presentation, surgical-series, and case-report evidence, but the mapping-level record cannot substitute for individual-case proof: determination requires urodynamic documentation, lesion-level imaging correlation, and review by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Urodynamic study (or documented catheterization dependence) characterizing the neurogenic bladder phenotype; MRI or surgical documentation establishing the conus lesion and its level; chronology establishing bladder dysfunction onset relative to the conus injury; workup excluding independent urologic disease (prostatic obstruction, stress incontinence, diabetic cystopathy); a medical professional's opinion connecting the documented findings in this individual case
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Benign prostatic hyperplasia or other bladder-outlet obstruction
Stress urinary incontinence from pelvic-floor weakness
Diabetic or other autonomic neuropathy causing cystopathy
Cauda equina syndrome with roots involved below the conus
Medication effects (anticholinergics, diuretics, sedatives) on voiding

suggestions.rationale: Authored conservatively at association-only strength: bladder dysfunction is a presenting sign of the syndrome itself, so a higher tier would partly restate the diagnostic picture; the edge records co-occurrence and leaves every individual determination to a qualified medical professional.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The defining-presentation and case literature documents bowel dysfunction among the core features of conus medullaris syndrome: the pure-conus definition used by the surgical literature is itself a combination of bladder/bowel incontinence and impotence signs (Chiu & Liao 2019), the lumbar burst-fracture case study documents bowel dysfunction from conus injury (Storch 2005), and the DAVF case report presents frank fecal incontinence as part of a rapidly progressive conus syndrome (Stevens 2009).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the evidence is case-report and small-series class with no population denominators, bowel dysfunction is defined as part of the syndrome's own presentation rather than an independently progressing condition, and anorectal-manometry quantification of conus-lesion bowel dysfunction is not reported in the available records, so only co-occurrence within the syndrome picture is recorded.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A sacral-defecation-control pathway is hypothesized: the S2-S4 Onuf nucleus and sacral parasympathetic outflow in the conus coordinate external-anal-sphincter tone, rectal sensation, and the defecation urge, so a conus lesion can simultaneously weaken voluntary squeeze, blunt rectal sensitivity, and dyscoordinate the rectoanal gradient, producing fecal seepage or frank incontinence that tracks the same lesion level as the bladder findings; recovery parallels sacral-segment viability rather than a progressive course. The mechanism is anatomically coherent and consistent with the presented cases, but the mapping-level evidence is case-report class without anorectal-physiology quantification, so only association is claimed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Bowel dysfunction co-occurs as a defining feature of conus medullaris syndrome in the presentation and case literature, but no anorectal-manometry cohort quantifies the outcome, so individual determination requires sphincter testing, lesion correlation, and review by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Anorectal manometry and endoanal imaging (or documented continence-product dependence) characterizing the fecal-incontinence phenotype; MRI or surgical documentation establishing the conus lesion and its level; chronology establishing bowel dysfunction onset relative to the conus injury; workup excluding independent anorectal disease (sphincter trauma, prolapse, diarrhea-predominant disorders); a medical professional's opinion connecting the documented findings in this individual case
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel or inflammatory bowel disease
Cauda equina syndrome with roots involved below the conus

suggestions.rationale: Authored conservatively at association-only strength: bowel dysfunction is a presenting sign of the syndrome itself and the quantified base is case-report class, so the edge records co-occurrence and leaves every individual determination to a qualified medical professional.
